commenti.body: In the initial parts, the film seems to suggest this idea of grace. As the film progresses this grace gives way to many contradictions and obscurities and in the end it is almost demystified or at least circumscribed. I think Perfect Days is a movie more complex and deep than what it seems.

I honestly think this idea that Hirayama is unhappy or suffering is largely manufactured by online discourse. I think that’s super inaccurate, and the Hirayama character is actually something of a Prince Myshkin. The depth of the movie comes with his interactions with other characters, not Hirayamas own personal struggles. It’s putting this positive, happy force into the world and seeing how it touches those around them. 

Wim Wenders himself said in an interview

 “He's actually a happy man. He's doing everything he likes. He listens to his music. In the evening, he reads a book. He goes to the public bath because his modest apartment doesn't have a bathroom. And he's amazingly content with everything he does and with everything he has.”

Pretty much everything Wenders has said about the character has been about how content and happy Hirayama actually is. 

I think people really fixate on him crying, and his past, but part of that grace is him moving past it.

Is not there? We watched different movies! ☺ Directors and actors promote the movie and for sure they don't make spoilers about the ending, especially if it evolves in unexpected ways. To spoil the drama of Hirayama is like to spoil Christie novels. Oh, I forgot to hide my spoiler, sorry! 😊

I'm sure I listened an interview where Wenders give a little vague clue about the fact that not everything is like it seems and something happens that challenge Hirayama or the audience. I'll share when I find it. 
I understand that Wenders wants to indulge the optimistic feelings of the widest audience. I wonder how people have absolutely no doubts about after the surprising and unexpected progression until the dramatic explicit end. 

It's like religion, people search for an easy exit way from harsh reality. When you say children that Father Christmas doesn't exist, they cry or simply ignore the truth and keep believing in Father Christmas, until they grow! 

To believe that a director like Wenders can indulge in the same way of life as Hirayama is like to believe in fairy tales! Usual words to promote the movie and indulge the audience that doesn't link to the dramatic end of the movie. If they prefer to believe is a Disney tale and cannot link to the metaphors, why disappoint them?

I’m not sure why you are equating positivity in art with a Disney tale? You do realize not every piece of art is a profound fight against the system?

Regardless, if you go into it, there is an inherently positive approach that Hirayama is taking. He is a toilet cleaner. He is not ashamed of this, regardless of some people overlooking him or ignoring him. He is an ex businessman and an ex alcoholic (these are the words of the director, not my own analysis). He is content. Another such way Wenders described the movie is his first movie about a peacemaker, and how to achieve peace, you must give up on growth and become content with yourself. He described Hirayama as his first “peacemaker”. 


Also, the people seeking out a directors opinion are not the people who need to be coddled into a Disney ending. I’d be interested if you could find that vague quote you’re referring to. I truly believe that you are over analyzing for the sake of over analyzing

"I truly believe that you are over analyzing for the sake of over analyzing"
That's offensive! Can you discuss without judging me, please? Have I judged or confronted you? Are we talking of movies or ourselves? 

"I’m not sure why you are equating positivity in art with a Disney tale?"
I did so? This is your tendency to judge me instead of talking of the topic. 

"You do realize not every piece of art is a profound fight against the system?"
I told so? Are you sitting on the teacher desk? Is that the way to discuss with people you don't know? 

Please, be polite if you want to keep talking
